prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, bringing atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are the one candidate on which all eight openings agree on the names and on which nobody disputes the principal credit. The magic-wavelength idea (Katori) and its realisation at record accuracy (Ye) gave quantum mechanics of real atoms a quantitative, reproducible expression: many independent laboratories (RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA, NIST, PTB, SYRTE and others) agree at the 1e-18 level, and comparisons over fibre links make the result verifiable rather than merely claimed. It enables tests of relativity at millimetre scales and searches for varying constants, and it ties closely to measured spectra, which is how I judge theory and experiment. In my opening I placed the topological insulators first and this clock fifth. Reading my colleagues has changed my ranking: the broad support, the clean two-name attribution and the maturity are stronger than I weighted them, whereas my own first choice carries an attribution problem that I underrated.
statement.case_against: A materials theorist should state the reservation honestly: some will see this as a precision-engineering advance rather than the discovery of a new state of matter or new physics, and the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 ion-trap prize have already covered part of the metrology narrative. Its fundamental-physics reach (dark matter, constants, redefinition of the second) is still largely prospective. Support is also broad but shallow in places: only two members ranked it first, and Mehlig ranked it last of his eight. Finally, if the committee prefers a verified new quantum state in real materials, B021 or B024 is a more natural fit with my own field, and I would not argue against that strongly.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the optical lattice clock first as clean, original, precision-driven quantum mechanics, but she asks whether it is sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-trap prizes; she also ranks topological insulators sixth, citing contested credit (Bernevig, Zhang, Fu, Moore) and overlap with the 2016 prize.
responses.response: I agree with her on both points and they have moved me. On the clock, I think the distinction is real: the comb gave a ruler for optical frequencies and the lattice clock exploits a new trapping idea (the magic wavelength) that makes many atoms interrogated at once without systematic shifts, which is a different physical insight. I would keep Ye's description careful so that it does not read as a comb prize. On B021 I concede her point on credit: Kane, Mele and Molenkamp are defensible, but a prize that leaves out Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang and the three-dimensional work would be hard to defend, and I raised that doubt myself in my opening. That is why I no longer put it first.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first and topological insulators second, valuing simple general mechanisms that made a whole field; he sees B024 as ripe, with robust flat-band correlated phases despite the open pairing question, and ranks the clock last of eight, citing overlap with 2005 and that its fundamental-physics impact is prospective.
responses.response: I share his taste for a simple mechanism, and B024 was my own second choice. Where I differ is on maturity. Eight years after the experiments, with the pairing mechanism unresolved, large sample-to-sample variation, and a credited set that omits Cao and other groups (Dean, Young, Yazdani and others), I would prefer to wait. DFT and tight-binding agree on the flat bands, which is reassuring, but the superconductivity is exactly the part that a Nobel citation would be expected to rest on. I also take his point that the clock's reach into fundamental physics is still partly prospective, but its core result, a measured and repeatedly confirmed 1e-18 uncertainty, is in hand and does not depend on those future payoffs.

responses.point: Olsson ranks spherical-aberration correction first as a genuine invention with wide impact in materials, catalysis and quantum materials; she rates twisted bilayer graphene as possibly premature (rank 6) and warns, regarding the Higgs, against treating leadership as equivalent to discovery.
responses.response: I am sympathetic to B011 from the materials side: aberration-corrected microscopy has changed what I can compare my calculations against, and its reproduction is as robust as any. My hesitation is the open question she raises herself, the STEM corrector line (Krivanek and collaborators) against the TEM correctors of Rose, Haider and Urban, which makes the three-name allocation less settled than the clock's. It also has only her support, so I would like to hear from her whether she thinks Krivanek can be handled with a citation worded around TEM aberration correction. I fully endorse her caution on the Higgs: a leadership-based credit for ATLAS and CMS is not the same as the decisive measurements, and she is right to ask for care.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the optical lattice clock first as the clearest case of a new measurement technique changing what can be observed, in the tradition of the 2005 comb and 1989 and 2012 precision-spectroscopy prizes, and argues that originality, clarity and breadth of consequence are all high, with maturity making recognition timely and arguably overdue.
responses.response: I agree with his reading on maturity and on the two-name configuration, and the tradition he cites is a fair one. My qualification concerns his phrase that it is the clearest case of a technique changing what can be observed: the same could be said of aberration correction or atom interferometry, so I would rely on the independent agreement across laboratories rather than on tradition. Atom interferometry (B035), his second choice, has a more entangled credit story because of Chu's absence, which makes the clock the simpler configuration.

uncertainties: Whether the committee is willing to treat a metrological advance as a discovery in the sense of the statutes, given the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-trap prize.
Exact priority among lattice-clock groups (Katori, Ye, Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley, Lisdat and others), which I have recalled from memory and not verified.
Whether Ye's potential later credit for the thorium nuclear clock (B058, outside this shortlist) should affect the timing of this award.
If the committee prefers a condensed-matter prize, whether B021 can be given a defensible three-person set that addresses Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and the three-dimensional topological insulators.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for the shortlisted candidates. My Uppsala and Los Alamos links and my work in density functional theory and magnetism do not connect to Katori, Ye, Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, MacDonald, Bistritzer or Jarillo-Herrero as far as the profile shows; I have not verified any personal ties beyond the profile.
